title: Users Per Acquisition Channel
description: Return the count of users in each acquisition channel. Output columns: acquisition_channel, user_count. Sort by user_count descending, then acquisition_channel ascending.
expected_query: SELECT acquisition_channel, COUNT(*) AS user_count FROM users GROUP BY acquisition_channel ORDER BY user_count DESC, acquisition_channel ASC
solution_query:
SELECT acquisition_channel, COUNT(*) AS user_count
FROM users
GROUP BY acquisition_channel
ORDER BY user_count DESC, acquisition_channel ASC;
explanation: Group the users table by acquisition_channel and count rows per group with COUNT(*). The dataset has 600 users spread across six channels plus a NULL group (15 users whose channel is unknown). Including the NULL group in the output is intentional — a real marketing KPI dashboard should surface unmapped users so the team can investigate, not silently discard them. The two-level ORDER BY (user_count DESC, acquisition_channel ASC) ensures the result is deterministic when two channels have equal counts.
hints: Think of this as a per-segment distribution: you want to know how many users fall into each distinct category — not a single total across all users.

Once you have the count per category, apply a two-level ORDER BY — primary by count descending so the largest segment appears first, secondary by channel name ascending to break ties deterministically.

title: Events Per Event Name
description: Return the count of events of each type. Output columns: event_name, event_count. Sort by event_count descending, then event_name ascending.
expected_query: SELECT event_name, COUNT(*) AS event_count FROM events GROUP BY event_name ORDER BY event_count DESC, event_name ASC
solution_query:
SELECT event_name, COUNT(*) AS event_count
FROM events
GROUP BY event_name
ORDER BY event_count DESC, event_name ASC;
explanation: Group the events table by event_name and count rows per group. The four event types (view_product, add_to_cart, start_checkout, purchase) form a natural funnel — this count-per-type query is the first step in any product funnel analysis. The result shows that view_product is by far the most common event and purchase is the least common, reflecting expected funnel drop-off. The two-level ORDER BY produces a deterministic ranking.
hints: This is a frequency analysis over an event stream: you want to know how many times each distinct event type occurred — not a global count across all events.
After computing the per-type counts, apply a two-level ORDER BY — descending by count so the most frequent event appears first, ascending by name to break ties deterministically.

title: Sample Easy: Total Completed Order Amount
description: Return the sum of `net_amount` for completed orders as total_completed_amount.
expected_query: SELECT SUM(net_amount) AS total_completed_amount FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed'
explanation: Filter to completed orders, then sum net_amount.
hints: This asks for a single aggregate value from a qualifying subset of rows — identify which condition defines the qualifying rows before deciding what aggregate to apply over them.

Apply the row-level condition before aggregating: rows that do not meet the status condition should never contribute to the total, so exclude them at the row level rather than adjusting after the fact.

title: Sample Medium: Users With No Orders
description: Return user_id and name for users who have never placed an order.
expected_query: SELECT u.user_id, u.name FROM users u LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.user_id WHERE o.order_id IS NULL ORDER BY u.user_id
solution_query:
SELECT u.user_id, u.name
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.user_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL
ORDER BY u.user_id;
explanation: LEFT JOIN keeps all users; users without matching orders have NULL order_id values.
hints: You want to find users who have zero matching rows in the orders table — this requires preserving all users first and then identifying those with no counterpart in orders.

Join users to orders in a way that keeps all users regardless of whether they have orders. After the join, users with no orders will have null values in the orders columns — filter on that null to isolate the unmatched ones.

title: Sample Medium: Revenue By Status
description: Return each order status and the total `net_amount` for that status.
expected_query: SELECT status, SUM(net_amount) AS revenue FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status
solution_query:
SELECT status, SUM(net_amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY status
ORDER BY status;
explanation: Group by status, then sum net_amount within each status.
hints: Every order belongs to exactly one status — you want one revenue total per status category, not a single global total.
Include all statuses rather than filtering to one — the breakdown emerges naturally from grouping, giving you the complete picture of how revenue is distributed across the order lifecycle.

title: Sample Medium: Monthly Revenue
description: Return month and revenue, grouped by month from orders.
expected_query: SELECT strftime(CAST(order_date AS DATE), '%Y-%m') AS month, SUM(net_amount) AS revenue FROM orders GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
solution_query:
SELECT strftime(CAST(order_date AS DATE), '%Y-%m') AS month, SUM(net_amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
explanation: Bucket by month using strftime with format '%Y-%m', then aggregate net_amount per bucket.
hints: Revenue needs to be broken out by calendar month, but raw timestamps do not group into months automatically — the first step is converting each order's timestamp into its month.
Use a date-conversion expression as the grouping key: it collapses all timestamps within the same calendar month into a shared bucket. Format the output as YYYY-MM strings.

title: Revenue Quartile Within Country
description: For each user with at least one completed order, assign them to a revenue quartile within their country (1 = lowest quartile of that country's user revenues, 4 = highest). Return user_id, country, total_revenue (rounded to 2 decimal places), and revenue_quartile. Sort by country ascending, then revenue_quartile descending, then user_id ascending.
expected_query: WITH user_revenue AS (SELECT o.user_id, u.country, ROUND(SUM(o.net_amount), 2) AS total_revenue FROM orders o JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.user_id WHERE o.status = 'completed' GROUP BY o.user_id, u.country), quartiled AS (SELECT user_id, country, total_revenue, NTILE(4) OVER (PARTITION BY country ORDER BY total_revenue) AS revenue_quartile FROM user_revenue) SELECT user_id, country, total_revenue, revenue_quartile FROM quartiled ORDER BY country ASC, revenue_quartile DESC, user_id ASC
solution_query:
-- Step 1: Aggregate completed orders to user-level revenue
WITH user_revenue AS (
    SELECT
        o.user_id,
        u.country,
        ROUND(SUM(o.net_amount), 2) AS total_revenue
    FROM orders o
    JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.user_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY o.user_id, u.country
),
-- Step 2: Assign revenue quartile within each country
quartiled AS (
    SELECT
        user_id,
        country,
        total_revenue,
        NTILE(4) OVER (
            PARTITION BY country
            ORDER BY total_revenue
        ) AS revenue_quartile
    FROM user_revenue
)
SELECT user_id, country, total_revenue, revenue_quartile
FROM quartiled
ORDER BY country ASC, revenue_quartile DESC, user_id ASC;
explanation: Two-CTE approach: user_revenue aggregates completed orders to one row per user (joined to users for country). The second CTE applies NTILE(4) partitioned by country — this produces per-country quartiles, not global ones. Without PARTITION BY country, NTILE(4) would bucket users globally, making a US user in quartile 3 incomparable to an AU user in quartile 3. Countries with fewer than 4 users are handled gracefully: NTILE distributes users left-to-right into the lower buckets, so a country with 2 users gets quartiles 1 and 2. The ORDER BY country ASC, revenue_quartile DESC, user_id ASC shows the highest earners within each country first.
hints: Break this into two stages: first collapse orders to a per-user revenue total (one row per qualifying user), then compute each user's relative position within their own country's revenue distribution — not their global position.

The relative-position step requires partitioning by country so each country's users are ranked independently. The aggregation must happen before the partitioned ranking — the window function cannot operate on raw order rows.

title: Monthly Order Coverage Per User
description: For every user, return one row per calendar month from their signup_date (truncated to month) through the latest order_date in the dataset (truncated to month) — including months when the user placed no orders. Return user_id, month (formatted YYYY-MM), and orders_in_month (count of orders placed in that month across all statuses; 0 if no orders). Sort by user_id ascending, then month ascending.
expected_query: WITH months AS (SELECT CAST(gs AS DATE) AS month FROM generate_series(DATE_TRUNC('month', (SELECT MIN(signup_date::DATE) FROM users))::DATE, DATE_TRUNC('month', (SELECT MAX(order_date::DATE) FROM orders))::DATE, INTERVAL '1 month') t(gs)), user_months AS (SELECT u.user_id, m.month FROM users u CROSS JOIN months m WHERE m.month >= DATE_TRUNC('month', u.signup_date::DATE)::DATE), order_counts AS (SELECT user_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date::DATE)::DATE AS month, COUNT(*) AS orders_in_month FROM orders GROUP BY user_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date::DATE)::DATE) SELECT s.user_id, strftime(s.month, '%Y-%m') AS month, COALESCE(oc.orders_in_month, 0) AS orders_in_month FROM user_months s LEFT JOIN order_counts oc ON s.user_id = oc.user_id AND s.month = oc.month ORDER BY s.user_id ASC, s.month ASC
solution_query:
-- Step 1: Generate all calendar months in the dataset's date range
WITH months AS (
    SELECT CAST(gs AS DATE) AS month
    FROM generate_series(
        DATE_TRUNC('month', (SELECT MIN(signup_date::DATE) FROM users))::DATE,
        DATE_TRUNC('month', (SELECT MAX(order_date::DATE) FROM orders))::DATE,
        INTERVAL '1 month'
    ) t(gs)
),
-- Step 2: Build per-user spine (each user x months from their signup onward)
user_months AS (
    SELECT u.user_id, m.month
    FROM users u
    CROSS JOIN months m
    WHERE m.month >= DATE_TRUNC('month', u.signup_date::DATE)::DATE
),
-- Step 3: Count actual orders per (user, month) across all statuses
order_counts AS (
    SELECT user_id,
           DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date::DATE)::DATE AS month,
           COUNT(*) AS orders_in_month
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY user_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date::DATE)::DATE
)
-- Step 4: Left join spine to order counts; COALESCE fills gaps with 0
SELECT s.user_id,
       strftime(s.month, '%Y-%m') AS month,
       COALESCE(oc.orders_in_month, 0) AS orders_in_month
FROM user_months s
LEFT JOIN order_counts oc
    ON s.user_id = oc.user_id AND s.month = oc.month
ORDER BY s.user_id ASC, s.month ASC;
explanation: Three-CTE date spine approach. months generates every calendar month from the earliest user signup to the latest order date using generate_series. user_months cross joins each user with months, filtering to months on or after their signup month — producing that user's full timeline. order_counts aggregates all orders (all statuses) by user and month. The final LEFT JOIN from user_months to order_counts fills in missing months: when a user had no orders in a month, oc.orders_in_month is NULL, and COALESCE converts it to 0. Without the spine, users appear only in months where they placed orders, silently hiding the months with no activity — the pattern that cohort retention and activity analyses depend on.
hints: The orders table only contains rows for months when orders occurred — months with no orders are silently absent. You need to generate the complete set of months each user should have, then check which of those months have orders.

Build a per-user timeline by combining each user with every month from their signup month onward. Then join the actual order counts onto that timeline — so months with no orders yield zero rather than disappearing from the result.

title: Top User Per Month By Completed Revenue
description: For each calendar month present in the orders data, return the single user with the highest completed-order revenue that month. If two or more users tie for the highest revenue in a month, return the one with the lower user_id. Return month (formatted YYYY-MM), user_id, and monthly_revenue (rounded to 2 decimal places). Sort by month ascending.
expected_query: WITH monthly_user_revenue AS (SELECT user_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date::DATE)::DATE AS month, ROUND(SUM(net_amount), 2) AS monthly_revenue FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed' GROUP BY user_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date::DATE)::DATE), ranked AS (SELECT user_id, month, monthly_revenue, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY month ORDER BY monthly_revenue DESC, user_id ASC) AS row_num FROM monthly_user_revenue) SELECT strftime(month, '%Y-%m') AS month, user_id, monthly_revenue FROM ranked WHERE row_num = 1 ORDER BY month ASC
solution_query:
-- Step 1: Aggregate completed orders to (user, month) revenue
WITH monthly_user_revenue AS (
    SELECT
        user_id,
        DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date::DATE)::DATE AS month,
        ROUND(SUM(net_amount), 2) AS monthly_revenue
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY user_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date::DATE)::DATE
),
-- Step 2: Rank users within each month; secondary sort on user_id breaks ties deterministically
ranked AS (
    SELECT
        user_id,
        month,
        monthly_revenue,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
            PARTITION BY month
            ORDER BY monthly_revenue DESC, user_id ASC
        ) AS row_num
    FROM monthly_user_revenue
)
-- Step 3: Keep only the top user per month
SELECT strftime(month, '%Y-%m') AS month, user_id, monthly_revenue
FROM ranked
WHERE row_num = 1
ORDER BY month ASC;
explanation: Two-CTE approach: monthly_user_revenue aggregates completed orders to (user, month) level with revenue rounded to 2 decimal places. The ranked CTE applies ROW_NUMBER() partitioned by month and ordered by monthly_revenue DESC, user_id ASC. The secondary user_id ASC is the deterministic tiebreaker — without it, any tie between users produces non-deterministic output that depends on execution order. ROW_NUMBER() is used rather than RANK or DENSE_RANK because it always assigns exactly one row rank 1 per partition, even in a tie: the secondary sort makes the tie-break explicit rather than silent. The final WHERE row_num = 1 extracts the winner per month.
hints: Break this into two stages: first aggregate completed orders to (user, month) revenue totals, then identify the single top user per month — with a rule that makes ties resolve the same way every time.

The tiebreaker is load-bearing: a window function that ranks users within each month must include a secondary sort key to guarantee identical results regardless of row storage order. Without it, which tied user wins is undefined.
